Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i'm trying to get a writing prompt into one clear shape for a new little family-meal-calendar episode, not the finished episode itself. It should be about the Alvarez family putting together a shared calendar for dinners from Monday, October 12, through Sunday, October 25. Keep it as one independent fictional event, with connected paragraphs around the practical details rather than making it sound like a formal policy or a recipe collection. The central thing is the family coordinating who is available, what can be cooked, and how everybody will find the plan. They live in Alder Bay, and the calendar is for meals at Mara and Dev's house, which has a small kitchen table that fits six. There are seven relatives involved, so not everyone needs to be at every meal.

Mara Alvarez is the person maintaining the shared calendar, and Dev is her partner. Their children are Tessa, who is 15, and Mateo, who is 10. Mara's mother, Ruth, lives nearby and usually joins for dinner on Sundays. Mara's brother Jonah works evening shifts at the harbor clinic on Tuesdays and Thursdays, so don't put him down as a dinner cook on either of those nights. Their aunt Leonie lives across town and likes to come when the bus is running on schedule. Ellis is Jonah's adult son and is in the family group chat, but for this particular request the message and calendar link are for Leonie, not Ellis. Please make the intended recipient really clear rather than giving the impression that both of them should get the message. The episode can mention the group chat as where Mara has been discussing dates, but don't turn that into a second recipient.

There is a little reason for this calendar now: Dev has started a temporary early shift at the ferry terminal, and Mara has two late workdays in each week. The arrangement is only for these two weeks while they are trying out a more predictable dinner routine, not a permanent family rule. Mara can cook Monday and Wednesday in the first week, but Wednesday's dinner needs to be quick because Tessa has orchestra at 6:30. In the second week, Mara's late workdays are Monday and Thursday. Dev can make a simple meal on Tuesday, October 13, and Tuesday, October 20, as long as the plan doesn't depend on him getting home before 5:45. Jonah is free on the other evenings but should only be assigned a meal when his shift information allows it. Nobody has confirmed whether he can swap a shift, so don't write as if he has.

For the meals, keep the suggestions ordinary and useful for a family calendar, not a detailed set of recipes. Tessa is vegetarian, and the family has said the shared main dish should work for her rather than leaving her with a side dish. Mateo dislikes mushrooms. Ruth prefers a mild dinner and has a dental appointment on Friday, October 16, so she'd rather not have anything crunchy that night. There's a bag of frozen peas and two cans of chickpeas already in the pantry, and Dev has asked to use at least one of those items during the two weeks. He bought them for a meal that got postponed. The family normally has dinner around 6:15, except on orchestra night when eating closer to 5:45 would help. Don't make up further dietary needs or claim that anyone has agreed to a menu that is only being proposed.

I want the finished episode to show Mara actually trying to put the information in order: which dates are workable, where there is a snag, and what still needs an answer. A numbered section would make sense for the two calendar weeks, with dates and a short meal or planning note for each relevant evening. It shouldn't imply that all seven people attend each dinner. The entries can distinguish a proposed meal from a confirmed cook if the details support that distinction. The family needs to leave Sunday, October 18, open because Ruth is taking Tessa and Mateo to a matinee and hasn't said what time they will be back. Sunday, October 25, is the usual dinner at Mara and Dev's, with Ruth expected to join; Jonah has not yet replied about that date.

Please include a natural, ordinary piece of quoted speech from one family member that fits the situation, something like Mara saying, “If we put the late nights on the calendar now, I won't have to text everybody at five.” It can be that wording or another simple line consistent with the same facts, but it should sound like something a person would say, not a slogan. The episode should include the fact that Mara plans to send Leonie the calendar link once the first version is ready, and the prompt should retain the exact recipient instruction Leonie, not Ellis. Don't resolve open questions just to make the plan look tidy. In particular, Jonah's answer for October 25 and whether he can trade any shift are still unknown.

There is also a small practical detail about the calendar itself: Mara is using a shared family calendar on her phone, but Ruth prefers to have the dates written on the paper pad beside her refrigerator. Mara said she'd print the two-week view after making the entries. Mentioning that difference can show why the calendar has to be readable and why a link alone isn't how every relative will check it. The family has not chosen a permanent system, and the episode shouldn't claim that the trial has settled that question.

End with a final paragraph that adds distinct information rather than recapping the dinner assignments. It can focus on one concrete next step or remaining logistical detail, such as Mara checking the bus timetable before she sends Leonie the link, since Leonie may need that to decide which evenings she can attend.
